title: The Gospel of Mark Timeline
sub: Immediately · Mark's Own Architecture · Every Chapter, Chapter & Verse
desc: The shortest, fastest-moving Gospel, traced by its own structure: no infancy narrative, no genealogy, just action from verse one, hinged at Peter's confession in chapter 8 and ending, in the earliest manuscripts, on an unfinished sentence at an empty tomb. Entries marked ✔Mk note details found nowhere in the other Gospels.

eras.label: Era One · Mark 1:1-13
eras.name: Prologue — The Beginning of the Gospel
eras.dates: No genealogy, no infancy story: Mark opens mid-stride

events.title: John Prepares the Way
events.detail: Mark's very first word is ‘beginning’ (archē): no genealogy, no manger, just a prophet in the wilderness eating locusts and wild honey, quoting Isaiah and Malachi together as one voice. The whole Gospel starts running before it's finished introducing itself.

events.title: The Baptism of Jesus
events.detail: Mark's Greek says the heavens were literally torn open (schizomenōus): a harder verb than Luke's 'opened,' the same word used later for the temple veil at 15:38. Two tearings frame the whole Gospel.

events.title: The Temptation in the Wilderness
events.detail: Compressed to two verses: no forty-day dialogue with the devil like Matthew and Luke give. Mark alone adds one small, strange detail: He was 'with the wild beasts,' and angels ministered to Him.

eras.label: Era Two · Mark 1:14-3:6
eras.name: Authority in Galilee
eras.dates: Seven scenes, one word repeated over and over: immediately

events.title: The Kingdom Announced; Four Fishermen Called
events.detail: ‘The time is fulfilled’: Jesus' whole message compressed into one sentence, then he calls Simon, Andrew, James and John with zero backstory. They just leave their nets. Mark's favorite word, 'immediately' (euthys), appears twice in five verses and roughly forty times across the whole book, this Gospel never slows down to explain itself.

events.title: Authority in the Capernaum Synagogue
events.detail: His first public act in Mark is an exorcism, not a sermon, and the unclean spirit is the one who correctly names him first: 'the Holy One of God.' The crowd's own verdict, 'a new teaching with authority': is about what he does, not what he says.

events.title: A House Full of Healing, Then a Retreat to Pray
events.detail: Simon's mother-in-law healed, then the whole city at the door by evening, and at dawn Jesus slips away to pray, only to tell the disciples who track him down that preaching elsewhere is 'what I came out for.' A pattern for the rest of the book: acclaim, then withdrawal.

events.title: Cleansing a Leper
events.detail: Jesus touches him (itself remarkable, since contact with a leper was itself defiling under the law) and then sternly orders silence. The man proclaims it anyway, and Jesus can no longer enter towns openly. The first instance of what scholars call the 'Messianic secret': Mark's Jesus keeps trying to keep his identity quiet, and it keeps getting out.

events.title: The Paralytic and the Authority to Forgive
events.detail: Four friends dig through a roof rather than wait for the crowd to clear. Jesus answers the scribes' silent objection, 'who can forgive sins but God alone?', not with argument but with a visible miracle as the proof: the harder claim (forgiveness) validated by the easier-to-check one (walking).

events.title: Levi's Call; a Question About Fasting
events.detail: A tax collector follows him on the spot, the same way the fishermen did, and Jesus eats at his house with 'sinners' while the scribes complain. His answer folds two images together: he is the bridegroom whose wedding can't be a fast, and new teaching is new wine that will burst old wineskins.

events.title: Two Sabbath Fights, and a Plot to Kill Him
events.detail: Grainfields, then a withered hand healed in a synagogue, both times Jesus reframes the Sabbath itself ('made for man, not man for the Sabbath'). The chapter ends on the first real threat in the book: Pharisees and Herodians, normally opposed to each other, start plotting together how to destroy him, this early, over a healed hand.

eras.label: Era Three · Mark 3:7-6:6
eras.name: Parables and a Widening Mission
eras.dates: The Twelve are named, the crowds grow, and the family thinks he's lost his mind

events.title: Crowds by the Sea; the Twelve Named
events.detail: So many sick people press in that Jesus keeps a boat ready to escape the crowd. Then, on a mountain, he names twelve by hand (Simon becomes Peter, James and John become 'Sons of Thunder') with Judas Iscariot named last, already flagged as the one who will betray him.

events.title: 'Out of His Mind'; the Unforgivable Sin; True Family
events.detail: A classic Markan sandwich: his own family sets out to restrain him because people are saying he's lost his senses, the scribes accuse him of being possessed by Beelzebul in between, and the scene closes with Jesus redefining family itself, 'whoever does the will of God', while his mother and brothers wait outside.

events.title: The Sower, Explained in Private
events.detail: The same parable does two different jobs at once: a public story about seed and soil that anyone can hear, and, once the crowd disperses, a private explanation reserved for the Twelve, because 'to you has been given the mystery of the kingdom.'

events.title: A Lamp, Seed Growing Secretly, a Mustard Seed
events.detail: Three short parables, one theme: the kingdom starts hidden and grows on its own timetable, not the sower's: 'the soil produces crops by itself... he himself does not know' how. Only Mark includes the seed-growing-secretly parable at all; it isn't in Matthew or Luke.

events.title: Stilling the Storm
events.detail: Jesus asleep on a cushion in a swamping boat, woken by panicked disciples, and he rebukes the wind the same way he rebukes an unclean spirit: 'Silence! Be still.' Their fear afterward is bigger than their fear of the storm: 'who then is this?'

events.title: Legion and the Gerasene Demoniac
events.detail: A man living naked among tombs, uncontainable by chains, meets Jesus in Gentile territory across the lake. The demons' own name for themselves ('Legion, for we are many') and the two thousand drowned pigs make this the most vivid exorcism in any Gospel. The healed man wants to follow Jesus; instead he's sent home to tell his own story first.

events.title: Jairus's Daughter and the Woman with the Hemorrhage
events.detail: Another sandwich: a synagogue official begs for his dying daughter, a woman who has bled for twelve years touches Jesus' cloak in the crowd on the way, and by the time they reach the house the girl has died. Jesus keeps the Aramaic he actually spoke ('Talitha kum,' 'little girl, get up') one of several places Mark preserves the original words, translated for a Greek-speaking audience.

events.title: Rejection at Nazareth
events.detail: His own hometown takes offense at him ('is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary?') and Mark records something the other Gospels soften: Jesus 'could do no miracle there' beyond a few healings, and 'was marveling at their unbelief.'

eras.label: Era Four · Mark 6:7-8:21
eras.name: Mission, Herod, and Bread
eras.dates: Two feedings, one long flashback, and a repeated question about loaves

events.title: The Twelve Sent Out Two by Two
events.detail: Travel-light instructions (a staff, sandals, no bread, no bag, no money) and real delegated authority over unclean spirits. They go out preaching repentance and come back having anointed the sick with oil.

events.title: Herod and the Death of John the Baptist
events.detail: A long flashback bracketed by the sending and return of the Twelve (another Markan sandwich): Herod's birthday banquet, a rash oath, Herodias's daughter's dance, and John's head on a platter. Herod himself is left afraid that Jesus might be 'John, risen from the dead.'

events.title: Feeding the Five Thousand
events.detail: 'You give them something to eat': Jesus turns the disciples' own math problem (two hundred denarii of bread) back on them, then feeds the crowd from five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. The number of baskets echoes the number of disciples who just failed to think of this.

events.title: Walking on Water; Healings at Gennesaret
events.detail: Jesus intends to 'pass by' the struggling boat, language that echoes God passing by Moses and Elijah in the Old Testament, before getting in and calming the wind. Mark's own explanation for the disciples' terror is blunt: 'they had not gained any insight about the loaves, but their heart was hardened.'

events.title: Tradition of the Elders; Corban
events.detail: Pharisees challenge unwashed hands; Jesus answers by exposing a real legal loophole of the day, declaring money 'Corban' (dedicated to God) to avoid supporting your own parents, as exactly the kind of tradition that 'invalidates the word of God.'

events.title: What Defiles a Person
events.detail: 'There is nothing outside the man which can defile him', and Mark adds an editorial aside found nowhere in Matthew's parallel account of the same teaching: 'thus He declared all foods clean.' A quiet but consequential line for a Gospel usually read as written for a Gentile audience.

events.title: The Syrophoenician Woman
events.detail: Jesus, deliberately trying to stay hidden in Gentile Tyre, is found by a mother whose sharp reply, 'even the dogs under the table feed on the children's crumbs', turns his own hard saying back on him and gets her daughter healed at a distance, without Jesus ever seeing the girl.

events.title: 'Ephphatha': a Deaf Man Healed
events.detail: Another Aramaic word kept and translated ('Ephphatha,' 'be opened') alongside an unusually physical healing method: fingers in the ears, spit on the tongue. The crowd's verdict deliberately echoes Isaiah's promise about the messianic age: 'the deaf to hear and the mute to speak.'

events.title: Feeding the Four Thousand; the Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod
events.detail: A second feeding miracle, structurally identical to the first (seven loaves this time, seven baskets left over) immediately followed by Jesus warning the disciples in a boat, with real exasperation, that they still don't understand: 'having eyes, do you not see?' The two feedings function almost as a test the disciples keep failing.

eras.label: Era Five · Mark 8:22-9:50
eras.name: The Turning Point
eras.dates: A blind man healed in two stages frames the hinge of the whole Gospel

events.title: A Blind Man Healed in Two Stages
events.detail: Unique to Mark: Jesus' first attempt only partly works ('I see men, for I see them like trees, walking') and it takes a second touch before he sees clearly. Positioned exactly where the disciples' own spiritual sight is about to be tested, this is usually read as a deliberate acted parable for what happens next.

events.title: Peter's Confession at Caesarea Philippi
events.detail: 'But who do you say that I am?' Peter answers correctly, 'You are the Christ', and Jesus immediately orders silence. The exact center of the Gospel: everything before has asked who Jesus is: everything after turns toward Jerusalem and the cross.

events.title: The First Passion Prediction; Take Up Your Cross
events.detail: Jesus states plainly, for the first of three times, that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, and be killed. Peter rebukes him for it and is rebuked back ('Get behind Me, Satan') the same voice that just confessed him correctly now arguing against the way he must go.

events.title: The Transfiguration
events.detail: Six days later, on a mountain, Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John: Elijah and Moses appear, the cloud speaks the same words heard at the baptism, 'this is My beloved Son.' Coming down, Jesus orders silence again, this time with an explicit deadline: 'until the Son of Man rose from the dead.'

events.title: The Boy with the Unclean Spirit
events.detail: The disciples fail to cast out a spirit that has thrown a boy into fire and water since childhood; Jesus succeeds, and gives the reason for their failure directly: 'this kind cannot come out by anything but prayer.' The father's cry, 'I do believe; help my unbelief', is one of the most quoted lines in the Gospel.

events.title: The Second Passion Prediction; Who Is the Greatest?
events.detail: Jesus repeats the prediction of his death; the disciples respond by arguing about which of them is the greatest. He answers by setting a child in their midst, the least powerful person in that society, as the model of true greatness.

events.title: The Strange Exorcist; Salt and Stumbling Blocks
events.detail: John tries to stop someone casting out demons in Jesus' name because 'he was not following us': Jesus overrules him: 'whoever is not against us is for us.' A string of hard warnings about causing others to stumble follows, ending on the odd, memorable image of being 'salted with fire.'

eras.label: Era Six · Mark 10:1-52
eras.name: The Road to Jerusalem
eras.dates: Hard teachings on the way south, framed by two very different requests

events.title: Teaching on Divorce
events.detail: Pharisees test him with a legal question; Jesus goes past Moses' concession ('because of your hardness of heart') back to Genesis itself ('what God has joined together, let no man separate') then gives the disciples a stricter private ruling than the public one.

events.title: Let the Children Come
events.detail: The disciples try to keep children away from Jesus; he is indignant, and turns receiving-like-a-child into the standard for entering the kingdom at all: direct continuation of the child he set among them one chapter earlier.

events.title: The Rich Man and the Eye of a Needle
events.detail: A man who has kept every commandment since youth is told the one thing he lacks: sell everything and follow. Mark alone adds that Jesus 'loved him' before the hard word: he leaves grieving anyway, and Jesus' verdict to the stunned disciples is blunt: with people it is impossible, but not with God.

events.title: Rewards for Leaving All; the Third Passion Prediction
events.detail: Peter points out what they've given up; Jesus promises it back a hundredfold, with persecutions attached, in this age and the next. Then, walking ahead of the frightened disciples toward Jerusalem, he gives the most detailed of his three passion predictions: betrayal, condemnation, mocking, flogging, death, and rising on the third day.

events.title: James and John Ask for the Best Seats; a Ransom for Many
events.detail: Right after hearing he's about to die, two disciples ask for the seats of honor beside him in glory. Jesus' answer redefines greatness one more time, 'whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant', and states his own mission in its clearest single sentence: 'to give His life a ransom for many.'

events.title: Blind Bartimaeus Healed at Jericho
events.detail: A blind beggar shouts 'Son of David', a title no one else has used yet in Mark, and won't be silenced by the crowd. Unlike the two-stage healing back at Bethsaida that opened this whole section, this healing is instant, and Bartimaeus responds by doing exactly what the rich man could not: he follows Jesus on the road.

eras.label: Era Seven · Mark 11:1-12:44
eras.name: Jerusalem — Confrontation in the Temple
eras.dates: One week, and every authority in the city tries to trap him

events.title: The Triumphal Entry
events.detail: A borrowed, never-ridden colt, garments spread on the road, and the crowd's shout: 'Hosanna... blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David': read the moment as messianic even before Jesus says a word. He enters the temple, looks around at everything, and simply leaves for the night: an oddly quiet end to a loud entrance.

events.title: The Fig Tree and the Temple Cleansing
events.detail: A textbook Markan sandwich: Jesus curses a fig tree for having no fruit though 'it was not the season for figs,' then drives out the money changers and dove-sellers quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah together: 'a house of prayer for all the nations... a robbers' den', and the next morning the disciples find the fig tree withered from the roots. The acted-out judgment on the tree and the temple are meant to be read as one and the same act.

events.title: 'By What Authority?'
events.detail: Chief priests, scribes and elders demand to know his authority; Jesus answers a question with a question about John's baptism: was it from heaven or from men? He traps them in their own fear of the crowd until they refuse to answer at all.

events.title: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
events.detail: A vineyard owner sends servant after servant, then his own beloved son, and the tenants kill him too, hoping to seize the inheritance: a parable the religious leaders understand perfectly is aimed straight at them, and it only makes them more determined to arrest him.

events.title: Caesar's Coin; the Sadducees and the Resurrection
events.detail: Two separate traps in one chapter: Pharisees and Herodians ask about paying tax to Caesar ('render to Caesar... and to God the things that are God's'), then Sadducees, who deny any resurrection, pose a riddle about a woman married to seven brothers: Jesus answers from the burning bush itself, 'I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob... not of the dead, but of the living.'

events.title: The Greatest Commandment
events.detail: A scribe asks in apparent good faith, and gets a straight answer (love God fully, and love your neighbor as yourself) the only exchange in the whole Jerusalem confrontation that ends with Jesus complimenting the questioner: 'you are not far from the kingdom of God.'

events.title: David's Son and David's Lord; Beware the Scribes
events.detail: Jesus poses his own riddle from Psalm 110: how can the Christ be David's son if David himself calls him 'Lord'? He then warns the crowd against scribes who crave honor in public while quietly devouring widows' houses, a line that sets up the very next scene.

events.title: The Widow's Two Coins
events.detail: Watching people give at the temple treasury, Jesus singles out a poor widow's two small coins, worth almost nothing, as worth more than the large sums the rich are putting in, 'for they all put in out of their surplus, but she, out of her poverty, put in all she had.'

eras.label: Era Eight · Mark 13:1-37
eras.name: The Olivet Discourse
eras.dates: Jesus' longest speech in Mark, given privately to four disciples on a hillside

events.title: The Temple's Destruction Foretold; the Beginning of Birth Pains
events.detail: 'Not one stone will be left upon another': a prediction that would be fulfilled within a generation, in AD 70. Asked privately for a sign, Jesus starts with wars, earthquakes and famines, calling them only 'the beginning of birth pains,' and warns the disciples they will personally stand trial before governors and kings for his name.

events.title: The Abomination of Desolation; the Son of Man Coming
events.detail: A cryptic warning, 'let the reader understand' is Mark's own aside to whoever is reading the account aloud, triggers an order to flee immediately, no time even to grab a coat. The discourse escalates to cosmic imagery, sun and moon darkened, before the Son of Man comes 'in clouds with great power and glory' to gather the elect.

events.title: The Fig Tree Lesson; Stay Awake
events.detail: A final, deliberately unsettling note: 'of that day or hour no one knows, not even the angels... nor the Son, but the Father alone.' The discourse ends on a single repeated command, addressed past the four disciples to everyone: 'what I say to you I say to all: stay awake.'

eras.label: Era Nine · Mark 14:1-52
eras.name: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
eras.dates: Two days before Passover, betrayal is already in motion

events.title: Anointing at Bethany; Judas's Betrayal Arranged
events.detail: Another sandwich: the chief priests plotting to kill Jesus 'in secret' brackets a woman breaking an alabaster jar of nard worth a year's wages over his head. Jesus defends her against the disciples' outrage in words that have outlived the complaint: 'wherever the gospel is proclaimed... what this woman did will also be spoken of in memory of her', and then, in the very next verse, Judas goes to the chief priests to betray him.

events.title: Preparing the Passover; the Betrayer Named
events.detail: A man carrying a water jar (an unusual enough sight, since that was normally women's work, that it functions as a prearranged sign) leads two disciples to a furnished upper room. At the meal, Jesus names the betrayer only obliquely: 'one of the twelve, the one who dips with Me in the bowl.'

events.title: The Lord's Supper
events.detail: Bread and cup reinterpreted as body and 'blood of the covenant, poured out for many', language that reaches back to Sinai's covenant blood in Exodus 24, and a vow not to drink wine again until the kingdom of God comes.

events.title: Peter's Denial Foretold
events.detail: Walking out to the Mount of Olives, Jesus predicts that all of them will fall away, quoting Zechariah's shepherd struck down. Peter insists he never will; Jesus gives him an oddly precise counter-prediction (before the rooster crows twice, three denials) that Peter still rejects outright.

events.title: Gethsemane
events.detail: 'Abba, Father' (Mark keeps Jesus' own Aramaic address to God, the most intimate moment of prayer in the Gospel, right beside his plainest statement of dread: 'My soul is deeply grieved to the point of death.' Three times he returns to find Peter, James and John asleep; the third time he simply says it's too late) 'the hour has come.'

events.title: The Arrest; a Young Man Flees Naked
events.detail: Judas's kiss as the prearranged signal, a scuffle in which a servant's ear is cut off, and then everyone flees, including, in a detail found nowhere else in any Gospel, an unnamed young man who escapes the soldiers' grip only by leaving his linen sheet behind and running off naked. Scholars have debated this one strange verse for centuries; some read it as Mark's own quiet signature.

eras.label: Era Ten · Mark 14:53-16:8
eras.name: Trial, Crucifixion, and the Empty Tomb
eras.dates: From the high priest's courtyard to a stone already rolled away

events.title: Before the Sanhedrin
events.detail: False witnesses can't even agree with each other, until the high priest asks directly: 'are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?' Jesus answers as plainly as he ever does in Mark, 'I am', and adds Daniel's Son of Man imagery on top of it, which the high priest immediately calls blasphemy, tearing his own robes.

events.title: Peter's Threefold Denial
events.detail: Exactly as predicted: a servant girl, then bystanders, press Peter three times in the courtyard below, and by the third denial he's cursing and swearing he doesn't know 'this man.' The rooster crows a second time, Peter remembers the prediction word for word, and breaks down.

events.title: Before Pilate; Barabbas Released
events.detail: Pilate's own question, 'are You the King of the Jews?', gets the same careful non-answer Jesus gave the high priest. Pilate, aware the charge is really envy, offers to release Jesus under the Passover amnesty custom; the crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, chooses the insurrectionist Barabbas instead and demands crucifixion.

events.title: Mocked by the Soldiers
events.detail: A purple robe, a twisted crown of thorns, mock salutes of 'Hail, King of the Jews': an entire Roman cohort's cruelty aimed at a single, silent prisoner before they lead him out to be crucified.

events.title: The Crucifixion
events.detail: Simon of Cyrene, pulled from the crowd to carry the cross, is identified by Mark as 'the father of Alexander and Rufus': named as if the first readers would recognize them, a small, concrete detail that has never stopped inviting speculation. Jesus is crucified between two robbers, under a sign reading 'THE KING OF THE JEWS,' mocked by passersby and priests alike with the same taunt: 'He saved others; He cannot save Himself.'

events.title: The Death of Jesus; the Veil Torn
events.detail: Darkness for three hours, then Jesus cries out in Aramaic ('Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani,' 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me') the opening line of Psalm 22, kept untranslated in the text before Mark translates it for the reader. At his death the temple veil tears in two, echoing the heavens torn open at his baptism, and a Roman centurion, not a disciple, gives the Gospel's clearest human confession: 'Truly this man was God's Son.'

events.title: Burial by Joseph of Arimathea
events.detail: A member of the very council that condemned Jesus asks Pilate for the body (real personal risk, 'he gathered up courage') and lays it in a rock-hewn tomb before the Sabbath begins. Two women watch and note exactly where, setting up the very next scene.

events.title: The Empty Tomb
events.detail: The women arrive to anoint a body and find the stone already rolled away and a young man in white announcing the resurrection. In the earliest and most reliable manuscripts, Mark's Gospel ends right here, mid-sentence in effect ('they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid') no resurrection appearance, no closing scene. Verses 9-20, printed in most Bibles as a longer ending, are near-universally judged by textual scholars to be a later addition, written in a noticeably different Greek style, to soften that abrupt original stop.
